text:
maria-support: Customer PS-452 reports intermittent 429s since yesterday. They run multiple app instances behind a shared egress pool. Same API key on all instances, but only a subset of hosts started getting 429s after a traffic spike. Asking: do we ever attribute limits by egress IP ahead of API key or project?

sam-ps-eng: Repro notes from customer:
- all instances send header "Authorization: Bearer sk-prod-ABC"
- requests look identical at app level
- affected VMs share a different NAT gateway (pool B) vs unaffected (pool A)
- spike at 2026-03-16T22:14Z

maria-support: Attached sample error returned to customer: 
`{\"error\":{\"type\":\"rate_limit\",\"message\":\"Rate limit exceeded\",\"code\":429}}`

tom-sre: Quick checks: can you paste the raw request headers and the gateway X-Forwarded-For? Also need the exact timestamps of a 429 occurrence so we can map to our rate-limiter logs.

sam-ps-eng: Here is sanitized curl they ran to repro (works from bad host):
```
curl -v https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-prod-ABC" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{\"model\":\"rwd-13b\",\"input\":\"hello\"}'
```
Response: 429. From a good host same curl returns 200.

jess-engineering: A few hypotheses: 
1) We always attribute to API key when present. If the key is valid, quotas/buckets tied to that key should apply.
2) If the API key is missing/invalid or stripped by a proxy, we fall back to IP-based attribution.
3) We may also have project-level and org-level aggregate buckets that can be hit even when key-specific buckets are fine.

So possible scenarios: either the requests from pool B are reaching us with the key stripped/rotated (causing IP fallback), or pool B's egress IP is consuming a shared org/project bucket that is exhausted.

maria-support: Customer insists the key is present and the same on all VMs. They said a recent autoscaling event spun up VMs with a different egress gateway.

tom-sre: Actionable repro for us: from one of your bad hosts run `tcpdump` or capture the outbound TLS SNI/ALPN so we can correlate with our ingress logs. Also share a single request id from our side (x-request-id) when a 429 happens. That lets us look up the exact attribution decision.

sam-ps-eng: They provided an x-request-id: `req_202603162214_7f9a` which maps to 2026-03-16T22:14:32Z.

api-bot: Quota check: api_key=sk-prod-ABC bucket_status: OK (used 42/1000). project=proj-88 bucket_status: OK (used 980/2000). org=org-17 bucket_status: THROTTLED (used 20000/20000). Attribution: org-level aggregate exceeded -> 429.

jess-engineering: That bot output is useful — it indicates org-level-rate-limit was the immediate cause. Important nuance: when many hosts share one egress pool, your burst from pool B could push total org consumption over the org bucket even if individual API-key buckets are under limit.

maria-support: So outcome: sometimes hosts show 200 because their requests landed before org bucket hit the ceiling; others got 429 after bucket filled. Customer was surprised because they expected per-key isolation.

tom-sre: Follow-ups for ops team:
- confirm org bucket timeline around 22:14Z
- confirm whether we applied any emergency fallback (retries, token-throttling)
- check if pool B hosts send any extra traffic (health checks, telemetry) that could have amplified usage

jess-engineering: Docs note we should make clearer: we enforce multi-level quotas. Priority is not simple "first match wins" — org/project buckets act as global guards and can preempt valid key-level calls when exhausted. We should update KB and add an FAQ for customers running many hosts behind a single egress.

maria-support: For next steps with customer: ask them to stagger start-up bursts, enable backoff, or request increased org reserve. Also suggest they pin a smaller pool or request dedicated egress if they need deterministic behavior.

sam-ps-eng: Customer is also asking for a short repro they can run themselves to demonstrate the behavior. Proposed script (single-line heat test):
```
for i in {1..500}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-prod-ABC" https://api.redwood.example/v1/embedding & done
```
Run that from two separate hosts with the same key but different egress gateways and observe difference in returned 200 vs 429 distribution.

tom-sre: I'll pull rate-limiter metrics and add to the thread. If org bucket is the root cause we should close with the KB update + an Ops checklist for customers.

maria-support: Thanks — please @jess-engineering and @tom-sre for any infra changes or doc PRs. :thumbsup:

jess-engineering: Noted. I'll open a tiny docs PR with an example and the mitigation steps.

api-bot: Note: tracked internally as INC-2026-089 for audit and followup.
